title: Physical and chemical properties and changes; density
blurb: Classify matter, tell physical from chemical properties and changes, and calculate density to predict sinking or floating.
question: An antacid tablet fizzes in a glass of water, while a spoonful of sugar quietly disappears in another. Which is a chemical change, which is physical, and how can you tell?

teach.body: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. A pure substance is either an element (one kind of atom) or a compound (two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, such as H₂O or NaCl, separable only by chemical means). A mixture is physically combined, with a variable composition, and can be separated by physical means. Plain English: a compound is a recipe locked in; a mixture is a toss-together.

children.label: Element
children.sub: One kind of atom: O₂, Fe

teach.caption: A suspension's particles settle and can be filtered. A colloid's particles do not settle but scatter light (the Tyndall effect): milk, fog.

head: Method
Separates
Using
teach.caption: Decanting (pouring off a liquid) and centrifugation (spinning) are also physical separations.

teach.body: A physical property can be observed without changing what the substance is: color, odor, density, melting and boiling point, hardness, solubility, conductivity, malleability, state. A chemical property describes how a substance reacts: flammability, reactivity with acid or oxygen, tendency to rust, toxicity. Physical properties are intensive (independent of amount: density, boiling point, color) or extensive (depend on amount: mass, volume, length).

teach.caption: Cooking an egg, digestion, fermentation and a tarnishing coin are all chemical changes.

head: Sign
Example
teach.caption: One sign suggests a reaction; the real test is whether a new substance has formed.

teach.body: Density = mass ÷ volume, in g/mL or g/cm³ (1 mL = 1 cm³). Water is about 1.0 g/mL. An object denser than the fluid sinks; less dense, it floats. Density is intensive: a nail and an iron beam have the same density. Find an irregular solid's volume by water displacement. Water is unusual: ice is less dense than liquid water, so ice floats (water is densest near 4 °C).

Rosa, a nursing applicant in her prerequisite chemistry lab, weighs a stone at 50 g. She lowers it into a graduated cylinder: the water rises from 30 mL to 50 mL, so the stone's volume is 20 mL. Density = 50 g ÷ 20 mL = 2.5 g/mL. That is greater than water's 1.0 g/mL, so the stone sinks. Half the stone would still be 2.5 g/mL.

teach.text: Dissolving salt or sugar and melting ice are PHYSICAL changes, and bubbles in boiling water are just water vapor. Density does NOT depend on sample size. Air is a mixture; water is a compound. And ice is LESS dense than liquid water.

items: Elements and compounds are pure; compounds have a fixed ratio. Mixtures vary and separate physically.
Physical properties are observed without changing identity; chemical properties describe reactivity.
Physical change: same substance. Chemical change: new substance (gas, color, precipitate, heat or light).
Density = mass ÷ volume; water ≈ 1.0 g/mL; denser sinks, less dense floats.
Density is intensive; ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water.

summary: You can now classify matter as an element, compound or mixture, separate mixtures by physical methods and tell physical from chemical properties and changes. You can also calculate density, use water displacement and predict whether an object sinks or floats.

A.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
options: Ice cream melting in the sun
A.why: Rusting forms a new substance (iron oxide) with different properties, so it is a chemical change.

whyNot.0: Melting changes only the state; the ice cream is still the same substance.
whyNot.1: Dissolving sugar is physical: the sugar molecules are still sugar and can be recovered by evaporation.
whyNot.2: Boiling turns liquid water into water vapor, the same substance in a different state.

A.q: Which of the following is a chemical property?
A.why: Flammability describes how a substance reacts (burns), which can only be observed by changing it chemically.

whyNot.0: Density is measured without changing the substance: a physical property.
whyNot.2: Boiling point is observed through a change of state, which is physical.
whyNot.3: Solubility is a physical property: dissolving does not create a new substance.

A.q: Which of these is a heterogeneous mixture?
A.why: Sand and water are not uniform throughout: the sand is visible and settles, so it is heterogeneous.

whyNot.1: Salt water is a solution, a homogeneous mixture that is uniform throughout.
whyNot.2: Air is a homogeneous mixture (a gas solution) of nitrogen, oxygen and other gases.
whyNot.3: Distilled water is a pure compound, not a mixture.

B.q: A 45 g sample has a volume of 15 mL. What is its density, and will it sink or float in water?
B.why: Density = 45 g ÷ 15 mL = 3.0 g/mL. That is greater than water's 1.0 g/mL, so it sinks.

whyNot.0: 0.33 g/mL divides volume by mass; density is mass ÷ volume.
whyNot.1: 3.0 g/mL is correct, but anything denser than water (1.0 g/mL) sinks.
whyNot.3: 675 multiplies mass by volume instead of dividing.

B.q: Which property stays the same no matter how much of the sample you have?
B.why: Boiling point is an intensive property: a drop and a pot of water boil at the same temperature.

whyNot.1: Mass is extensive: more sample, more mass.
whyNot.2: Volume is extensive and grows with the amount of sample.
whyNot.3: Total heat (thermal) energy grows with the amount of sample, so it is extensive.

B.q: A lab technician needs to separate two liquids that have different boiling points. Which method should she use?
B.why: Distillation heats the mixture so the liquid with the lower boiling point vaporizes first and is collected after condensing.

whyNot.0: Filtration separates an undissolved solid from a liquid, not two mixed liquids.
whyNot.1: Decanting pours a liquid off a settled solid or a separate layer; it does not use boiling points.
whyNot.2: Chromatography separates substances by how fast they travel through a medium, not by boiling point.

C.q: A student mixes two clear, colorless solutions. A cloudy yellow solid forms and settles. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: A physical change, since no gas formed
A chemical change, since a precipitate formed
A physical change, since both were liquids
A chemical change, since the mix is heterogeneous
C.why: A precipitate, a new insoluble solid appearing when solutions mix, is a sign that a new substance formed.

whyNot.0: Gas is only one sign of a reaction; a precipitate is another, so no gas does not rule out a chemical change.
whyNot.2: Starting as liquids says nothing about whether a new substance formed.
whyNot.3: Sand in water is heterogeneous without any reaction; the evidence here is the new solid.

C.q: Which statement about compounds and mixtures is correct?
options: Air is a compound of nitrogen and oxygen
A compound's makeup varies sample to sample
Mixtures need chemical reactions to separate
Water is a compound with a fixed H:O ratio
C.why: A compound has a fixed ratio of elements: every water molecule is H₂O, two hydrogens to one oxygen.

whyNot.0: Air is a mixture: its gases are not chemically bonded and its composition can vary.
whyNot.1: A variable makeup describes a mixture; compounds have a fixed ratio.
whyNot.2: Mixtures separate by physical means; compounds need chemical means.

C.q: A 27 g metal ring is dropped into a graduated cylinder, and the water level rises from 20.0 mL to 23.0 mL. What is the ring's density?
C.why: Volume by displacement = 23.0 − 20.0 = 3.0 mL. Density = 27 g ÷ 3.0 mL = 9.0 g/mL.

whyNot.0: 1.2 g/mL divides by the final water level (23 mL) instead of the volume displaced.
whyNot.1: 1.4 g/mL divides by the starting water level (20 mL) instead of the change.
whyNot.3: 0.11 g/mL divides volume by mass; density is mass ÷ volume.

reteach.title: Kitchen chemistry
reteach.question: In a kitchen you can chop, melt, dissolve, toast and bake. Which of these make something new, and which only change its look?

blocks.body: Chop a carrot and it is still carrot. Melt butter and cool it, and it is butter again. Stir sugar into iced tea, and evaporating the tea would leave the sugar: all physical. Now toast bread or bake a cake: the brown crust, new smell and new texture come from new substances, and you cannot un-toast toast. That is a chemical change. Ask: is it the same stuff in a new form, or new stuff?

blocks.text: Heat alone does not decide it. Boiling water is physical; frying an egg is chemical. Look for a new substance.

explain.body: Elements: one kind of atom. Compounds: elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio. Mixtures: physically combined, variable makeup; homogeneous (uniform) or heterogeneous (not uniform).

items.label: air, salt water, sand in water

test.q: Table salt, NaCl, is best classified as:
test.why: NaCl is sodium and chlorine chemically combined in a fixed 1:1 ratio: a compound.

whyNot.1: An element has one kind of atom; NaCl contains two.
whyNot.2: A solution is a homogeneous mixture; NaCl dissolved in water would be one, but NaCl itself is a compound.
whyNot.3: A colloid is a mixture whose particles stay dispersed; pure NaCl is not a mixture.

explain.body: Physical change: form or state changes, same substance (melting, cutting, dissolving). Chemical change: new substance, often shown by gas, color change, a precipitate, heat or light, or a new odor.

test.q: Which observation is evidence of a chemical change?
options: A glass shattering on the floor
An antacid tablet fizzing in water
test.why: The fizzing antacid releases a new gas (carbon dioxide) from a reaction: a new substance.

whyNot.0: Boiling bubbles are water vapor, the same substance in a different state.
whyNot.1: Shattered glass is still glass: a physical change in shape.
whyNot.3: Dissolving salt is physical; the salt is recovered if the water evaporates.

explain.body: Density = mass ÷ volume. Water is about 1.0 g/mL. Denser objects sink and less dense ones float. Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats; water is densest near 4 °C.

test.q: Why does ice float on liquid water?
options: Frozen water has lost some mass
Ice is less dense than liquid water
Ice is a different compound from water
Ice has more mass per unit of volume
test.why: As water freezes, hydrogen bonding spreads the molecules into an open structure, so ice is less dense and floats.

whyNot.0: Freezing is a physical change; no mass is lost.
whyNot.2: Ice and liquid water are the same compound, H₂O, in different states.
whyNot.3: More mass per unit of volume means more dense, which would make ice sink.

explain.body: Solution: homogeneous, particles never settle. Suspension: particles settle and can be filtered (sand in water). Colloid: particles stay dispersed but scatter light, the Tyndall effect (milk, fog).

test.q: Milk scatters a flashlight beam, and its particles stay dispersed instead of settling. Milk is best described as:
test.why: Particles that stay dispersed yet scatter light (the Tyndall effect) mark a colloid.

whyNot.0: A true solution does not scatter a light beam.
whyNot.1: A suspension's particles settle out over time; milk's do not.
whyNot.2: Milk is a mixture of many substances, not a single compound.
